chapters.title: Chapter 5: Beyond Equality: KKT Conditions and Inequality Constraints

children.text: This is the final round. The interviewer hands Ananya the exact Stock X and Stock Y problem from Chapter 4, still with the no-short-selling rule now bolted on, and asks her to solve it properly, not just note that the unconstrained answer is infeasible. This lesson builds the tool: the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, four rules that together solve any problem mixing equality and inequality constraints at once.

body.text: KKT conditions are four rules that any solution to a constrained problem, equality and inequality constraints together, must satisfy simultaneously. Solve all four at once and you have solved the problem, exactly generalizing what the Lagrangian already does for equality constraints alone.

children.text: Write every inequality constraint in the standard form g(x) ≤ 0 (no-short-selling, -wi ≤ 0, already fits this shape). A problem with p inequality constraints and m equality constraints gets one multiplier per constraint of each type.

body.caption: The standard form for a mixed equality-and-inequality problem.
The generalized Lagrangian. ν handles equality constraints exactly as before; λ is new, one per inequality constraint.

children.text: The Four KKT Conditions, One at a Time
Stationarity is the familiar one: the gradient of the Lagrangian, with respect to x, must vanish, exactly as in Chapter 4.
Primal feasibility just says the candidate solution has to actually obey every constraint it was given, nothing new conceptually, just now spelled out for both types at once.

body.latex: g_i(\mathbf{x}^*) \leq 0 \text{ for all } i, \qquad h_j(\mathbf{x}^*) = 0 \text{ for all } j
body.caption: 2. Primal feasibility.

children.text: Dual feasibility is genuinely new: every inequality multiplier must be non-negative. Equality multipliers can be any sign, but inequality multipliers cannot, because their sign encodes a real direction. A binding inequality constraint can only ever be costing you something relative to the unconstrained answer, never helping, so relaxing it can only help or do nothing, never hurt. That one-directional logic is what forces the multiplier's sign.
Complementary slackness is the condition that formally encodes the binding versus non-binding idea from the previous lesson, in a single, elegant equation per constraint.

body.caption: 4. Complementary slackness. Either the multiplier is zero (constraint slack), or the constraint sits exactly at its boundary (constraint binding). Never both nonzero at once.
The four KKT conditions at a glance

children.text: Applying KKT to the No-Short-Selling Case
Write the minimum variance problem with n stocks, a budget constraint, and no short-selling on every stock. gi(w) = -wi ≤ 0 for each i, and h(w) = wᵀ·1 - 1 = 0.

body.caption: Stationarity, with λ the vector of multipliers on the -wi ≤ 0 constraints.

body.text: This gives a clean rule for every single stock: either wi = 0 and lambda_i is free to be positive (the no-short rule binds, the stock is excluded), or lambda_i = 0 and wi is free to be positive (the rule does not bind, and stationarity for that stock reduces to 2(Sigma w)i = nu, exactly the Chapter 4 equation, as if the inequality were never there at all). Every stock in the portfolio falls into exactly one of these two camps at the solution.

children.text: Solving the Stock X / Stock Y Hedge Example via KKT

Chapter 4 found the unconstrained answer wants wX ≈ -57%, violating wX ≥ 0. Hypothesis: this constraint binds, so wX = 0, and by the budget rule, wY = 1. Check every KKT condition against this candidate.

body.caption: Using σX² = 0.16, σY² = 0.04, σXY = 0.072 from Chapter 4.
Since Y is unconstrained (positive weight), its stationarity equation pins down nu directly.
Solving X's stationarity equation for lambda_X, using nu just found.

body.text: Every condition checks out, so this is confirmed as the true KKT solution: hold nothing in Stock X, put everything in Stock Y. With shorting off the table, there is no way left to hedge X's extra volatility, so the best move is simply not to hold it at all. For exactly two assets, this candidate happened to be reachable by clamping the violating weight to zero and letting the budget rule fill in the rest. With three or more assets, that shortcut generally fails, because the capital freed up by clamping one weight needs to be reallocated optimally across the remaining stocks jointly, not just handed to whichever stock is left. The next lessons work through that fuller case properly.

body.title: Check complementary slackness
body.question: At a candidate KKT solution for a long-only minimum variance portfolio, stock A has weight wA = 0.08 (strictly positive) and its associated inequality multiplier comes out to λA = 0.03. Does this satisfy complementary slackness?
options: No, because λA should be zero whenever wi is positive, and here λA = 0.03 ≠ 0, so this violates complementary slackness
Yes, because both wA and λA are positive, so their product is automatically zero
Yes, complementary slackness only applies to the budget constraint, not individual weights
Cannot be determined without knowing the other weights
body.explanation: Complementary slackness requires λi × wi = 0 for every i. If wA is strictly positive, meaning the no-short-selling constraint is not binding for that stock, λA must be exactly zero. A nonzero λA alongside a strictly positive wA is inconsistent, and signals this cannot be a valid KKT point as given.

body.title: Interpret a positive multiplier
body.scenario: At a correctly solved long-only minimum variance portfolio, one stock has weight exactly zero, and its associated multiplier is λ = 0.05.
body.prompt: Using the shadow-price interpretation from Chapter 4, what would relaxing this particular no-short-selling constraint, allowing a small short position, do to the portfolio's minimum variance? Why must λ be non-negative for this to make sense?
body.modelAnswer: Since this constraint is binding, weight exactly zero, with a positive multiplier, relaxing it, allowing a small short position, would reduce the minimum achievable variance, by roughly lambda times the size of the relaxation, the same shadow-price logic from Chapter 4. This is exactly why dual feasibility requires lambda greater than or equal to zero: a binding inequality constraint can only be costing you relative to what an unconstrained solver would find, never helping you. A negative lambda would imply the constraint is somehow making the objective better, a contradiction, since removing a rule can never make an already-optimal point worse.

cards.definition: ∇f + Σλi∇gi + Σνj∇hj = 0. The gradient balance condition, extending Chapter 4's directly.
Every constraint, equality and inequality alike, must actually be satisfied by the candidate solution.
λi ≥ 0 for every inequality multiplier. Encodes that a binding inequality can only cost you, never help.
λi · gi(x*) = 0 for every i. Either the constraint binds (sits exactly on its boundary) or its multiplier is zero, never both nonzero at once.

points: KKT conditions are four rules, stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness, that together solve any problem mixing equality and inequality constraints.
Dual feasibility, λi ≥ 0, is new to this chapter: it encodes that a binding inequality constraint can only cost you relative to the unconstrained answer, never help.
Complementary slackness, λi·gi(x*) = 0, formally captures the binding versus non-binding distinction from the previous lesson in a single equation per constraint.

Applied to no-short-selling, each stock falls into exactly one of two camps at the solution: excluded (wi = 0, λi free to be positive) or held (wi free to be positive, λi = 0, behaving exactly like Chapter 4's unconstrained case for that stock).

For the Stock X and Stock Y hedge example, all four KKT conditions confirm the correct long-only answer is wX = 0, wY = 1: exclude the volatile, highly correlated stock entirely rather than hold any of it.

Clamping a violating weight to zero happened to work for exactly two assets here. With three or more stocks, the freed-up capital needs to be reallocated jointly and optimally, not just handed to whatever is left, which the next lessons work through.
